children: urged Taiwanese officials to reconsider the treatment of an employee accused of helping divert advanced AI hardware to China, Bloomberg News reported Sunday. The case is testing the company’s oversight of its distribution network as authorities scrutinize suspected violations of chip export restrictions.
The employee, identified by his surname Chang, is among nine defendants charged in Taiwan. Prosecutors allege the network shipped 74 servers containing Nvidia
chips to China and attempted to move another 56 before Taiwan’s Coast Guard intercepted them in May. Chang faces forgery and breach-of-trust charges.
For investors, the proceedings raise questions about Nvidia’s

compliance controls and exposure to tighter export enforcement. Greater scrutiny could complicate sales through intermediaries and increase compliance costs, while Taiwan’s central role in manufacturing Nvidia
chips makes relations with its authorities particularly consequential.
said its internal investigation found no evidence that Chang knew about the alleged diversion by employees of other companies. People familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that Nvidia
challenged the charges in discussions with political officials, who said they could not intervene in judicial proceedings.

Prosecutors accuse Chang of helping obtain approval for 130 server sales to a Taiwanese infrastructure provider that lacked adequate installation space. They also allege he concealed the buyer’s financial shortcomings and funding from a Chinese entity. The allegations remain subject to trial.

Taiwan plans to bring its chip export restrictions closer to Washington’s rules. The case illustrates the difficulty of tracking advanced processors through multiple buyers and resellers, and the growing pressure on Nvidia
to explain how it evaluates customers.

title: Nvidia defends employee in Taiwan AI chip smuggling case
